verdicts.evidence: I attacked the tax arithmetic and it moves the answer up, not down. The Revenue Act of 1942 did replace the 35-60 percent graduated excess-profits schedule with a flat 90 percent rate - but it paired that with two features that both raise the after-tax cost of a deductible dollar, and the claim's method names one of them and then declines to act on it. (1) An overall ceiling limited combined normal tax, surtax and excess-profits tax to 80 percent of surtax net income. (2) A post-war refund credit of 10 percent of the excess-profits tax. The NBER's own marginal-tax-rate methodology computes the ceiling case explicitly as R = 0.8 x 0.9 = 0.72, i.e. a 72 percent effective marginal rate and a 28-cent after-tax cost per deductible dollar. The full grid of cases: 90 percent rate with the credit ignored = 10 cents; 90 percent with the credit valued = 19 cents; at the 80 percent ceiling with the credit ignored = 20 cents; at the ceiling with the credit valued = 28 cents. So the realistic range is 10-28 cents, the modal cases cluster at 19-20 cents, and the claim's ci80 top of 25 cents excludes the ceiling-plus-credit case that the standard methodology computes. The claim's own method concedes 'secondary accounts of the period settle on the government might pay up to 80 percent, implying about 20 cents' and then sets the central at 15 anyway - a downward pull with nothing behind it.
